course.title: How to Use LLMs
course.subtitle: A practical course distilled from Andrej Karpathy's segmented talk on working with language models.
course.description: Learn what happens inside an LLM chat, how to judge its stored knowledge, and how to keep conversations focused. Then practice choosing models and using search, research, uploaded sources, code tools, generated diagrams, and coding agents with appropriate verification.
course.attribution: Based on Andrej Karpathy's segmented talk. Citations use the source segment and timestamp format (seg NN, MM:SS); product names, prices, and model availability reflect the talk's recording context.

lessons.title: How an LLM chat works
lessons.summary: A chat is a shared token stream that grows turn by turn; its contents are the model's working context. The model's learned knowledge and assistant persona come from training, while tools are supplied by the surrounding application.
objectives: Describe how user and model turns append to a token sequence.
Explain why the conversation is called a context window.
Distinguish pre-training from post-training.
Recognize the knowledge cutoff and tool limits of a model answering from its weights.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Think of a chat as a one-dimensional stream of tokens. You add a message and press Enter; control passes to the model, which appends its reply until it emits an end-of-turn marker. The app then hands control back to you. The accumulated exchange is the context window: the conversation's working memory, directly available to the model (seg 01, 00:07–00:54).

sections.heading: Where the model comes from
sections.html:
Pre-training compresses patterns from internet text into model parameters through next-token prediction. Karpathy uses a lossy, probabilistic “zip file” as an analogy: it captures patterns and associations, not an exact searchable archive. Post-training uses human-built conversations to shape an assistant persona. Knowledge and conversational style are both baked into the resulting model (seg 01, 01:13–02:29; 03:40–04:24).

Because pre-training is costly and infrequent, a model's stored knowledge has a cutoff. New events need to be brought into the conversation through a tool or supplied source. A base model also has no calculator, browser, or Python interpreter unless the application provides those tools (seg 01, 02:31–03:07; 03:23–03:37; 04:28–05:02).

sections.heading: How to use the mental model
sections.html:
1. Start a chat to open a fresh token sequence.
  2. Give the model the relevant request; each turn becomes part of the shared context.
  3. Remember that the answer is generated from learned patterns plus the current context, not retrieved from a perfect archive.
  4. For current facts or exact computation, supply evidence or use an application tool that can retrieve or calculate.

Popular facts are more likely to be represented well than rare details. Treat fluent delivery and a friendly persona as separate from factual reliability (seg 01, 05:57–06:09).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• The “zip file” analogy does not mean exact recall; the learned representation is lossy and probabilistic.
  • A cutoff is structural: recent events may not be in the model's weights.
  • Do not assume the model itself can browse, calculate, or run code; tool access belongs to the surrounding application.
  • Assistant tone is a result of post-training, not evidence that an answer is correct.

quotes.text: When we click new chat, we begin a token sequence.
Together, we are building out the token stream, which we also call the context window.
You're talking to a zip file.

takeaways: A chat is a sequence of tokens appended by both sides.
The context window is the model's working memory for the current exchange.
Pre-training supplies learned patterns; post-training shapes assistant behavior.
Use supplied sources and tools for information outside the model's reliable recall.
practice: Open a new chat and ask a question that depends on today's news; note whether the app uses a search tool or answers from memory.
Ask the model to explain the difference between a context window and model training in its own words.

lessons.title: Knowledge queries & trust
lessons.summary: A raw model is most useful for facts that are both not recent and extremely common online. Treat answers as fallible recollections and scale verification to the stakes.
objectives: Apply the talk's age-and-frequency test to a knowledge question.
Explain why an answer from model weights is not a citation.
Choose a primary source for checking a claim.
Set verification effort in proportion to the consequences of error.

sections.heading: The two-part test
sections.html:
Before asking the model to answer from its learned knowledge, ask whether the information is not recent and extremely frequent on the internet (seg 02, 00:27–00:56). Karpathy illustrates this with a common caffeine question; the model gives an approximate answer from its weights without a search.

That answer is a probabilistic recollection, not a guarantee. Common facts are more likely to be represented well because the model encountered many references to them (seg 02, 01:01–01:21; 02:28–02:45).

sections.heading: Verify against evidence
sections.html:
When accuracy matters, compare the answer with a primary source. In the medicine example, Karpathy checked the ingredient list on the actual NyQuil box rather than relying on the model's confident description (seg 02, 02:16–02:27). The point is a process: use the answer as a lead, then inspect authoritative evidence yourself.

For low-stakes, common information, light checking may be enough. For high-stakes information, verify thoroughly; the model's fluency does not change the cost of being wrong (seg 02, 03:07–03:15).

sections.heading: A practical trust checklist
sections.html:
1. Is the fact recent? If so, use a current source instead of relying on stored knowledge.
  2. Is it common and widely discussed, or obscure and niche?
  3. Ask for the basis of the answer, then verify important claims against a primary source.
  4. For product ingredients or medical details, inspect the package or official information directly.
  5. Spend more effort checking when the consequences of error are higher.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• “It said so” is not evidence; the model itself may be unsure or wrong.
  • Polish and confidence do not replace recency and frequency as clues to likely recall quality.
  • Do not skip verification of dosage, ingredient, or other consequential details.
  • Low stakes can justify lighter checking, but not treating every answer as guaranteed.

quotes.text: I'm not guaranteed that this is the correct answer. This is just its vague recollection of the internet.
I actually took out the box and I looked at the ingredients and I made sure that NyQuil ingredients are exactly these ingredients.
This is just probabilistic statistical recollection of the internet.

images.caption: Check whether a fact is recent before relying on stored model knowledge.
Compare consequential details with the source itself.
Calibrate the amount of checking to the stakes.

gifs.caption: Test whether a knowledge question is old and ubiquitous.
Verify details against the primary source.

pitfalls: A model answer is not a source citation.
Common, old information can still be misstated.
Ingredient and medical claims need first-hand checking.
Low stakes justify lighter verification, not blind trust.
takeaways: Use the raw model for old, widely represented facts.
Think of answers as recollection rather than retrieval.
Verify important claims against primary sources.
Increase checking effort as stakes rise.
practice: Ask for a stable, common fact and a recent fact; identify which requires a current source.
Choose a claim in an answer and find the official or primary source that could confirm it.

lessons.title: Start a new chat per topic
lessons.summary: Treat conversation context as working memory with a cost. Starting fresh at topic changes removes irrelevant tokens that can distract the model and add computation.
objectives: Describe the two costs of a long, irrelevant context.
Decide when a topic change calls for a fresh chat.
Carry forward only material relevant to the next task.
Recognize when related context should remain available.

sections.heading: Context is a resource
sections.html:
Karpathy's default is simple: when you switch topics, start a new chat (seg 03, 00:00–00:16). A new chat resets the context window to zero. That is useful when the old conversation no longer helps with the next question.

Accumulated tokens have an accuracy cost: irrelevant history can distract the model and reduce accuracy on later turns. They also have a compute cost: a larger window makes token generation slower and slightly more expensive (seg 03, 00:16–01:04).

sections.heading: Keep useful context, discard stale context
sections.html:
Think of the context window as working memory. Keep the current task's relevant facts and instructions; do not preserve a sprawling conversation merely because some detail might become useful someday. The practical goal is to keep context as short as you can, which Karpathy says can make a session faster and slightly better (seg 03, 01:04–01:21).

There is a clear exception: if prior information is genuinely related to the current task, leave it in context. A fresh chat is a hygiene rule for topic switches, not a demand to erase relevant background (seg 03, 01:21–01:31).

sections.heading: How to apply the rule
sections.html:
1. Notice when the conversation has moved to a different subject.
  2. Start a new chat for that subject.
  3. Restate or paste only the context the new task needs.
  4. Keep working in the existing chat when its history directly supports the task.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Long context is not free: it can add distraction as well as latency and cost.
  • Do not keep one giant chat just in case; unused tokens are still present now.
  • Context clutter is described as a model behavior, not merely a user-interface inconvenience.
  • Do not remove relevant background that the current task depends on.

quotes.text: Any time you are switching topic, I encourage you to always start a new chat.
think of the tokens in the context window as a precious resource.
keep it as short as you can. And you can expect that to work faster and slightly better.

images.caption: A fresh chat resets the context window.

Keeping a chat open for hypothetical future use carries a present cost.
Irrelevant context may distract the model on later turns.
Prune only information that is not relevant to the current task.
takeaways: A new chat resets working context.
Use a fresh chat when the subject changes.
Carry over only the material needed for the new task.
Retain relevant context when a task genuinely continues the prior one.
practice: Review a long chat and list which facts a new, unrelated question would actually need.
Begin a fresh conversation for a different topic and compare the context you must restate.

lessons.title: Models & pricing tiers
lessons.summary: Know which model and plan are answering before judging the result. Providers trade model capability against compute cost, and plans differ in included models, limits, and price.
objectives: Find and confirm the active model before a task.
Explain why larger models may cost more.
Compare plans using their included models and usage limits.
Describe the ‘LLM council’ approach to comparing providers.

sections.heading: Check the active model
sections.html:
Karpathy's first habit is to check the model selector and know which model is responding (seg 04, 00:02–00:12). In his recording, a logged-out session could silently provide a smaller model without identifying it, so do not assume that the product name alone tells you which capability is active (seg 04, 00:24–00:48).

Model names and availability change. The talk's comparisons—such as GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini, and Grok 3—describe the lineup at the time, not a current pricing guide.

sections.heading: What tiers buy
sections.html:
More capable models generally cost more to compute, which is why providers charge more for access to them (seg 04, 02:12–02:27). Plans can differ in the models included, message caps, and added features. Read the current plan details and fine print instead of relying on a remembered headline price.

Choose the most powerful model that works for your needs and budget. Casual use may be well served by a lower tier; professional use may justify paying for a stronger model if the added capability saves enough time (seg 04, 02:22–02:47).

sections.heading: Compare answers
sections.html:
Karpathy sometimes asks several models the same question and compares their responses, an approach he calls his “LLM council” (seg 04, 04:25–04:51). Use comparison to reveal differences in reasoning or suggestions; multiple answers do not automatically prove which one is correct.

  1. Confirm the model name.
  2. Check the current plan's model access and usage limits.
  3. Match the model tier to the task's difficulty and your budget.
  4. For consequential facts, still verify against evidence.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Do not assume a free or logged-out session is using the flagship model.
  • Names, tiers, prices, and limits in the talk are time-bound examples.
  • A higher price does not make every answer correct.
  • Agreement among models is not a substitute for checking a primary source.

quotes.text: keep in mind what model you are actually using.
the bigger models are more expensive to calculate. And so therefore, the companies charge more for the bigger models.
I kind of refer to all these models as my LLM council.

images.caption: Check which model is active, especially in logged-out sessions.
Match the plan and model capability to the work.
Comparing providers can surface different responses.

pitfalls: Do not assume the model selector is on the strongest option.
The talk's provider lineup, prices, and plan limits may have changed.
Paying more does not remove the need to verify answers.
Several agreeing models do not replace primary evidence.
takeaways: Check the active model before interpreting an answer.
Plans vary by model access, usage limits, and price.
Choose capability in relation to task and budget.
Compare models when useful, then verify important claims independently.
practice: In your preferred chat app, locate the active model and current plan limits.
Ask two available models the same low-stakes question and compare how their answers differ.

lessons.title: Thinking models
lessons.summary: Reasoning modes spend extra time deliberating before answering. Use them for tasks that benefit from additional effort, while accounting for latency and checking their output.
objectives: Describe how a thinking mode differs from an immediate response.
Identify task types Karpathy associates with extended thinking.
Choose when the extra time is worthwhile.
Maintain verification even when a model presents a reasoning process.

sections.heading: What thinking mode does
sections.html:
Some models or modes deliberate before producing the final answer. The extra reasoning time can help on problems that need multiple steps, such as difficult math or coding (seg 05; see also seg 08, 00:58–01:27). It is a choice about spending more inference effort, not a guarantee of correctness.

Karpathy connects this “thinking” behavior to the thinking half of deep research, where the system searches and reasons over a longer run (seg 07, 00:37–00:45).

sections.heading: When to spend the time
sections.html:
Use a thinking mode when the task is complex enough that a quick response is unlikely to be sufficient. For a simple lookup or straightforward request, a slower mode may add little value. Consider both the task and the time available.

When comparing modes, give them the same problem and evaluate the usefulness and correctness of the result. If there is a verifiable answer, check it independently; extra deliberation is still generated model output.

sections.heading: A practical workflow
sections.html:
1. Estimate whether the problem needs several reasoning steps.
  2. Select a thinking or extended-thinking option for a hard math, coding, or analysis task.
  3. Allow for the added wait.
  4. Inspect the final result and test it against a known answer, source, or execution environment when possible.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Do not assume a longer wait means the result must be correct.
  • Do not spend extra time on tasks that need only a simple response.
  • A displayed reasoning process does not replace independent verification.

quotes.text: in the process of reinforcement learning, the model discovers thinking strategies that lead to good outcomes.
So the model will try out different ideas. It will backtrack. It will revisit assumptions.
There exists a class of models that we call thinking models.

images.caption: Thinking modes spend additional time before responding.
Reserve extended deliberation for tasks that benefit from it.
A longer process still calls for checking the result.

pitfalls: Deliberation can take longer without guaranteeing correctness.
A thinking mode may be unnecessary for simple requests.
Reasoning output should be checked against evidence or execution where possible.
takeaways: Thinking modes trade time for additional model deliberation.
They are most useful for harder multi-step tasks.
Choose the mode based on task complexity and wait tolerance.
Verify the answer even after extended reasoning.
practice: Give a simple and a multi-step problem to normal and thinking modes; compare time and useful differences.
Check a reasoning-mode answer with a calculator, source, or runnable example.

lessons.title: The internet search tool
lessons.summary: Search adds current web material to the model's context. The application searches, loads fetched pages as text, and lets the model resume answering with that evidence.
objectives: Trace how a search result reaches the model's context.
Recognize when a query calls for web search.
Ask for evidence-backed answers from current sources.
Verify that citations support the claims they accompany.

sections.heading: How search changes the chat
sections.html:
An LLM by itself is a self-contained model with a cutoff. With a search tool, the application can stop generation, search the web, fetch pages, load their text into the context window, and let the model continue answering from that material (seg 06, 01:50–02:07). The fetched pages become part of the working context, alongside the conversation.

Search is useful for facts that are recent, changing, or niche—areas where stored knowledge may be missing or unreliable (seg 06).

sections.heading: Use search deliberately
sections.html:
Tell the assistant when the answer must be current and ask it to use search. Then inspect the cited pages yourself, especially when the result affects an important decision. Search can retrieve evidence, but the model can still misread a page or make an unsupported claim.

  1. State what needs to be current or sourced.
  2. Ask the model to search and summarize the relevant pages.
  3. Open citations and confirm they support the specific claim.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Do not treat a search icon as proof that every answer was grounded in sources.
  • A citation can be present while a claim is inaccurate or unsupported.
  • Search results may be incomplete; inspect the underlying page and its context.

quotes.text: It's inert, it's closed off, it's got no tools. It's just a neural network that can emit tokens.

when the model emits the search the internet token, the chat GPT application… will stop sampling from the model and it will take the query that the model gave, it goes off, it does a search, it visits web pages
you can actually visit those web pages yourself and you can make sure that these are not hallucinations from the model

pitfalls: Search results are material to inspect, not automatic proof.
Citations can accompany hallucinated or misinterpreted claims.
Search may not retrieve every useful source.
takeaways: Search can bring information newer than model training into context.
Fetched pages are returned as text for the model to use.
Ask explicitly for search when recency matters.
Open citations and check the supporting passage.
practice: Ask a current question and request web search; open a citation and find the exact passage supporting one claim.
Compare a search-grounded answer with a memory-only answer to a stable fact.

lessons.title: Deep research
lessons.summary: Deep research combines repeated internet search with extended reasoning to produce a cited, report-length answer. Its duration and citations do not remove the need to check sources and figures.
objectives: Explain the combination of search and thinking in deep research.
Choose a research question suited to a long-running report.
Check whether report citations support their claims.
Identify inconsistencies in tables, calculations, and prose.

sections.heading: What it is for
sections.html: Karpathy describes deep research as internet search combined with thinking, running for a long time. It can spend tens of minutes collecting and synthesizing material into a cited, research-paper-like report (seg 07, 00:37–00:45). Use it when a question needs multiple sources and a substantial synthesis rather than a quick lookup.

sections.heading: Review the report as a draft
sections.html:
Citations make a report easier to inspect, but they do not guarantee that claims are correct. Karpathy found a table of US LLM labs where the report had incorrect material despite citations; his point is to verify the sources and the details (seg 07, 06:25–07:01). Check whether a cited source actually supports the adjacent statement, and independently recalculate figures when needed.

Use the report as a research starting point: follow the sources, look for contradictions, and distinguish sourced facts from the model's synthesis.

sections.heading: Workflow
sections.html:
1. Write a focused question that benefits from several sources.
  2. Ask deep research for a cited synthesis.
  3. Review the report's structure, source list, and claims.
  4. Open citations for important statements and check figures against their source.
  5. Revise or narrow the question where the sources disagree or leave gaps.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• A long research run can still produce incorrect claims.
  • Citations do not guarantee that a table or number is accurate.
  • Do not accept a report without checking whether its sources support the claims.

quotes.text: Deep Research is a combination of internet search and thinking and rolled out for a long time.
So this is not a simple and short response. This is kind of like almost like a custom research paper on any topic you would like.
Treat this as your first draft. Treat this as papers to look at. But don't take this as definitely true.

pitfalls: Long runtime does not ensure accuracy.
Citations can be attached to a faulty claim or table.
Synthesis may blur source statements and model interpretation.
takeaways: Deep research combines search and extended reasoning.
It suits multi-source questions that need report-length synthesis.
Citations make checking possible but do not make checking optional.
Verify figures and tables against underlying sources.
practice: Request a short cited research report on a topic you know; inspect whether two citations support their claims.
Check one table entry against its source and note any mismatch.

lessons.title: File uploads: papers & books
lessons.summary: Supplying a paper or chapter puts concrete text into the model's context so it can answer from the source rather than hazy memory. Co-read actively, because summaries can miss details and large files can exceed limits.
objectives: Explain how uploaded document text enters context.
Set up an LLM-assisted reading session around a supplied source.
Recognize likely limits around figures and large files.
Check the model's interpretation against the original text.

sections.heading: Bring the source into the conversation
sections.html:
Instead of asking a model to recall a book or paper from training, provide the actual text. The application converts an uploaded PDF to text and loads that content into the token window; pasting a chapter can serve the same purpose (seg 08, 02:43–02:47). The supplied source gives the model something concrete to reference in the current conversation.

Karpathy describes using an LLM as a reading partner: start with a summary, then work through sections and ask questions where you get stuck. He says the approach improves his retention and understanding (seg 08, 04:22–04:30; 07:00–07:08).

sections.heading: Co-read rather than delegate
sections.html:
1. Upload a paper or paste the chapter text.
  2. Tell the model which work and section it is reading, then ask for an initial summary.
  3. Read one section at a time and ask questions when something is unclear.
  4. Compare explanations and summaries with the original passage.

Document text is not the same as perfect access to every page feature. Karpathy expects figures in PDFs may be dropped or poorly understood, and a large PDF can hit a chat length limit (seg 08, 02:19–02:42; 03:15–03:22). Treat those as practical constraints and check the source directly.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Do not ask for detailed chapter facts from memory alone when you can provide the text.
  • Figures and images may not survive document ingestion as usable evidence.
  • Large documents may exceed the model or chat's length limit.
  • A summary can be wrong; use the original passage as the authority.

quotes.text: we are providing the LLM with additional concrete documents that it can reference inside its context window.
this PDF is basically converted to a text file. And that text file is loaded into the token window.
I encourage you to experiment with it, and don't read books alone.

pitfalls: The model's learned memory of a particular book may be hazy.
Uploaded PDFs may lose figures or images in text extraction.
Large files can exceed chat length limits.
Do not delegate the entire reading; cross-check explanations with source text.
takeaways: An uploaded or pasted source adds concrete material to context.
Begin with a summary, then read and question section by section.
Ask about the passage where confusion occurs.
Check the model's interpretation against the source itself.
practice: Paste a short public-domain passage and ask for a summary plus three questions the passage answers.
Ask a follow-up about one sentence, then confirm the response against that sentence.

lessons.title: The Python interpreter
lessons.summary: When a problem exceeds direct pattern completion, an LLM can write a program for an attached interpreter, receive the result, and explain it. Tool access varies between models, so verify calculations rather than trusting plausible answers.
objectives: Describe the model-to-interpreter-to-model tool loop.
Distinguish simple arithmetic from calculation delegated to code.
Check whether a model has an execution tool available.
Verify close-but-wrong arithmetic independently.

sections.heading: A tool-use loop
sections.html:
Instead of answering directly, the model can emit a program for the application to run. The model pauses, the Python interpreter executes the code, and the result returns to the model as text for a final response (seg 09, 00:12–00:33; 02:26–02:44). Python is one possible language; Claude's example used JavaScript for calculation (seg 09, 04:20–04:29).

Simple arithmetic may be answered through learned pattern completion. Harder multiplication can reveal when a model uses code; the talk compares ChatGPT's interpreter with other models that attempt the calculation “in its head” (seg 09, 01:11–02:44).

sections.heading: Check for execution
sections.html:
Tool availability differs by product and model. A model without a code interpreter can still produce a plausible number, including one that is close but wrong. Karpathy's comparison includes examples from Grok 3 and Gemini 2.0 Pro where the observed response did not show tool use and arithmetic failed on harder problems (seg 09, 03:22–05:14).

  1. Use a task difficult enough to distinguish calculation from a memorized pattern.
  2. Ask the model to show or run code if the application supports it.
  3. Check the result with a calculator or another reliable method.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Do not assume every model has the same tools.
  • Pattern completion is not reliable arithmetic, even when the result looks plausible.
  • A close answer can still be wrong; independently check calculations.

quotes.text: instead of the LLM giving you an answer directly, it has the ability now to write a computer program
It's actually not really doing math. It's actually more like almost memory work
if they don't have the tools available, they'll just do their best, which means that they might hallucinate a result for you.

pitfalls: In-head arithmetic is pattern completion, not dependable computation.
Tool availability varies across models.
Close-looking outputs can still contain arithmetic errors.
takeaways: An application can run model-written code and feed the result back.
The model pauses during tool execution and resumes with the returned output.
Different models have different execution tools.
Verify arithmetic with an independent calculator or program.
practice: Ask a model to multiply two large numbers; see whether it invokes a code tool and check the result on a calculator.
Repeat with a second model and compare tool availability and accuracy.

lessons.title: Advanced Data Analysis
lessons.summary: Advanced Data Analysis can gather data, run code, plot results, and fit trends like a junior analyst. The talk's demo shows why you should inspect missing-data assumptions, generated code, and whether prose agrees with computed output.
objectives: Outline an end-to-end data analysis workflow with search and code.
Spot silent substitutions for missing values.
Compare narrative results with computed variables or plots.
Explain why reading generated code matters.

sections.heading: A collaborative analysis workflow
sections.html:
Karpathy describes Advanced Data Analysis as working with a junior data analyst: it can gather data, produce plots, fit curves, and extrapolate trends (seg 10, 00:04–00:19). In the demo, he explicitly asked ChatGPT to search for OpenAI valuation data, requested a table, then asked it to plot the values on a log scale (seg 10, 00:28–01:06).

  1. Ask for sourced data and specify that search should be used.
  2. Inspect the resulting table, including missing entries.
  3. Ask for the plot or analysis and examine the generated code.
  4. Check computed results before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: Audit assumptions and output
sections.html:
The demo's code silently replaced a 2015 “NA” valuation with 0.1, or $100 million, without explaining that assumption (seg 10, 01:32–01:46). In a later extrapolation, the prose answer said about $1.7 trillion while the plot label implied roughly $20 trillion. Asking it to print the variable exposed the discrepancy (seg 10, 02:29–03:24).

Read generated code to see how missing data is handled. For fitted trends, compare the narrative with the actual computed variable and remember that extrapolations depend on the chosen fit (seg 10, 02:12–02:29).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Missing values may be silently replaced with an assumption.
  • The prose answer can contradict a plot, label, or computed variable.
  • A trendline extrapolation depends on the selected fit and data.
  • If you cannot inspect the code, these failure modes are harder to catch.

quotes.text: it's kind of like did it without telling us. So it's a little bit sneaky.
I would be hesitant to potentially recommend the use of these tools if people aren't able to like read it and verify it a little bit for themselves.
So a lot of promise but be careful.

pitfalls: NA values may be silently converted into numbers.
A written result may disagree with the code's computed output.
Extrapolations rely on assumptions about the chosen fit.
Without code review, hidden choices are easy to miss.
takeaways: Ask explicitly for search when collecting current data.
Inspect tables for missing values before analysis.
Read code to find substitutions and assumptions.
Cross-check prose, plots, labels, and printed variables.
practice: Give a small table with one missing value to a data-analysis tool and inspect how it handles the gap.
Ask it for a calculation and a plot, then compare the prose answer to the underlying output.

lessons.title: Claude Artifacts & diagrams
lessons.summary: Claude Artifacts can turn supplied material into a small browser app, such as a flashcard tool, while Mermaid can render a conceptual diagram. These are useful bespoke aids with frontend-only limits.
objectives: Explain how an Artifact turns generated code into a browser interface.
Create a flashcard app from supplied study material.
Ask for a Mermaid conceptual diagram of a source.
Recognize the frontend-only and persistence limits described in the talk.

sections.heading: Custom apps in the conversation
sections.html:
Claude Artifacts let the model write code, such as a React component, that Claude's interface runs in the browser (seg 11, 00:17–00:34). Karpathy's flashcard demo starts with pasted text about Adam Smith, generates questions and answers, then asks Claude to build an app where the learner can reveal answers, mark them right or wrong, reset, and shuffle (seg 11, 00:27–01:59).

The shift is from configuring a general-purpose app to asking for a small, bespoke tool tailored to the material at hand (seg 11, 02:07–02:30).

sections.heading: Use diagrams to understand
sections.html:
Karpathy's most valuable Artifact use is conceptual diagram generation. Provide a chapter and ask for a conceptual diagram; Claude can write Mermaid definitions and render a graph of the ideas (seg 11, 03:06–03:44). A tree-like layout can make a chapter's argument easier to remember, and the same approach can be used for books, chapters, or source code (seg 11, 04:33–04:56).

  1. Supply source material in the conversation.
  2. Request a diagram of the relationships or argument, not just a list of terms.
  3. Inspect the rendered graph and correct relationships that do not match the source.

sections.heading: Limits and pitfalls
sections.html:
Artifacts are browser-side, frontend-only apps in the described workflow; Karpathy notes there is no backend or database (seg 11, 02:30–02:41). Treat them as one-off learning tools, not as persistent services. He also says he is not a daily Artifact user; his endorsement is specifically strongest for diagrams.

  • Do not assume a generated Artifact has server-side storage.
  • Check flashcards and diagrams against the supplied text.
  • Generated code and rendered relationships can still contain mistakes.

quotes.text: Claude just writes the app just for you and deploys it here in your browser.
There's none of that here. There's no database or anything like that.
the one use case that I did find very useful in my own work is basically the use of diagrams, diagram generation.

pitfalls: Artifacts described here are frontend-only, with no backend or database.
Do not assume study progress persists between sessions.
Verify flashcards and diagram relationships against the source.
Karpathy's endorsement is particularly about diagrams, not daily app use.
takeaways: Artifacts can make generated code run inside the browser interface.
A supplied text can become a bespoke flashcard app.
Mermaid diagrams can map conceptual relationships in source material.
Check generated learning tools against the original source.
practice: Paste a short text and ask Claude to make a flashcard Artifact; test whether each answer matches the source.
Ask for a Mermaid concept diagram of a chapter and mark one relationship to verify.

lessons.title: Cursor & vibe coding
lessons.summary: A coding agent in a desktop editor can work across a real project because it sees the file tree and can run commands. Vibe coding can accelerate iteration, but you remain responsible for inspecting changes, confirming risky commands, and testing the result.
objectives: Distinguish project-aware coding tools from web-chat code snippets.
Describe Composer's multi-file agent workflow.
Define vibe coding as Karpathy uses the term.
Identify review, command-confirmation, and manual fallback practices.

sections.heading: Work in the project context
sections.html: For professional coding, Karpathy says ordinary web chat lacks the context of the user's codebase. Dedicated desktop editors such as VS Code, Windsurf, and Cursor can reference files on disk and edit them in place (seg 12, 00:28–01:22). In the talk, Cursor calls Claude 3.7 Sonnet through Anthropic's API (seg 12, 01:28–01:55); treat those product details as recording-era context.

sections.heading: Composer and vibe coding
sections.html:
Cursor's Composer feature is described as an autonomous agent on the codebase: it can execute commands and change multiple files. In the demo, Karpathy asks it to scaffold a React tic-tac-toe app, then iterates with plain-language requests such as adding confetti when a player wins (seg 12, 02:03–02:52; 03:58–04:07).

Karpathy calls handing control to Composer, telling it what to do, and hoping it works “vibe coding” (seg 12, 04:16–04:28). That speed is useful, but the phrase captures the uncertainty: he says he is not keeping full track of every edit as it happens.

sections.heading: Keep the work reviewable
sections.html:
1. Open a project directory in the coding editor.
  2. Describe the desired change clearly and let the agent work on the project files.
  3. Review diffs and run the application to verify behavior.
  4. Read commands before confirming them, especially when they create or download assets.
  5. Keep good checkpoints; if the agent gets stuck, edit the local files manually.

The demo even adds a sound from a URL whose provenance Karpathy does not know. Inspect dependencies and assets rather than assuming generated additions are trustworthy (seg 12, 08:04–08:14).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• “Hoping it works” is not a substitute for reviewing edits and testing the application.
  • Do not blindly approve commands that the agent pauses to confirm.
  • Generated dependencies and downloaded assets may have unclear provenance.
  • Keep the ability to inspect and modify the files yourself.

quotes.text: the composer is like an autonomous agent on your code base, it will execute commands, it will change all the files as it needs to
vibe coding just refers to letting giving in giving control to composer and just telling it what to do, and hoping that it works.
worst comes to worst if we can't debug anything, we can always fall back to standard programming.

pitfalls: Project-aware agents can make broad multi-file changes that need review.
Do not blindly confirm commands when the tool pauses for approval.
Downloaded asset provenance may be unknown.
Vibe coding still requires running, inspecting, and validating the result.
takeaways: A coding editor can expose the project's file tree to an agent.
Composer can run commands and edit multiple files from plain-language instructions.
Review diffs and test the running application after changes.
Manual programming remains a fallback because project files are local.
practice: In a throwaway project, ask a coding agent for one small UI change; inspect the diff and run it.
Before accepting an agent-suggested command or asset, read what it does and where the asset comes from.

lessons.title: Voice input & output
lessons.summary: Speech-to-text dictation and text-to-speech read-aloud make ordinary text chats faster to use. Voice here is a wrapper around a text LLM, distinct from native audio conversation.
objectives: Distinguish dictation from voice mode
Use mobile dictation or system-wide desktop dictation
Use read-aloud or system text-to-speech
Recognize when technical terms should be typed

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Voice input converts speech to text before the text reaches the model; voice output reads the model's text response aloud. Text remains in the middle, so these tools make a text chat easier to operate rather than making the model audio-native.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Speaking is often quicker than typing, especially on a phone. Karpathy reports using speech for about half of his desktop queries and roughly 80% of his mobile queries.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html:
On mobile, use the microphone dictation control to put a transcript in the text box. On desktop, a system-wide dictation app can send text to whichever field is focused. For answers, use the app's read-aloud control or a system text-to-speech tool.

Type product names, library names, and code identifiers yourself when transcription accuracy matters.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Dictation is not the same as native audio conversation.
  • Speech recognition can garble proper nouns and technical identifiers.
  • Read-aloud availability differs between apps.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Try dictating a routine question, review the transcript before sending, and compare the time with typing. Then listen to a longer response with read-aloud.

quotes.text: the big takeaway here is don't type stuff out. Use voice. It works quite well and I use this pervasively

images.caption: Karpathy describes how often he uses spoken queries.
Mobile dictation turns speech into editable text.
Read-aloud sends a text response through speech synthesis.

pitfalls: Confusing dictation with native audio mode
Trusting transcription of technical names without checking
Assuming every chat app has read-aloud
takeaways: Dictation is speech-to-text feeding a text model.
Use voice when it is faster than typing.
Review transcripts, especially names and code terms.
Read-aloud is text-to-speech and may be app-specific.
practice: Dictate a question on your phone, inspect its transcript, and correct any errors before sending.
Try a system-wide dictation hotkey in a desktop text field, then listen to the answer with read-aloud.

lessons.title: Advanced voice mode
lessons.summary: Native audio models process audio tokens directly instead of placing speech-to-text and text-to-speech around a text model. Advanced voice can handle expressive speech, though behavior and availability vary.
objectives: Explain the difference between wrapped and native audio
Understand that audio tokens are the exchange medium
Try expressive voice interactions
Account for refusals and changing availability

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: In the talk's model, audio is represented as chunks of audio tokens and handled inside the language model. This differs from dictation, where speech is transcribed to text, and read-aloud, where text is synthesized into speech.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Direct audio input and output can preserve qualities such as voice and prosody without text as the intermediate exchange. A transcript shown in the interface may be generated afterward rather than being the actual conversation medium.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Choose the app's voice conversation control, which is distinct from its dictation microphone. Experiment with storytelling, speaking style, or a spoken explanation, and check the current app and account tier for access.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• A displayed transcript does not prove that text was the real-time medium.
  • Voice modes can refuse some requests inconsistently.
  • Feature availability and plan limits change over time.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Ask voice mode to explain a familiar topic aloud, then request a different speaking style. Treat the result as an interaction experiment, not a reliable test of every capability.

quotes.text: the voice is handled natively inside the language model... it can hear and speak directly in audio. There's no text involved whatsoever.
this text is after the audio. What actually was happening is there were audio tokens going back and forth

images.caption: Advanced voice is presented as audio handled within the model.
A demonstration of expressive spoken output.
Karpathy discusses the mode's limitations.

pitfalls: Treating a post-hoc transcript as the live exchange format
Expecting every request to be fulfilled
Relying on old plan or rollout information
takeaways: Native audio models work with audio tokens directly.
Dictation and read-aloud still route through text.
Voice can add expressive, conversational interaction.
Check current availability and expect occasional refusals.
practice: Compare dictation-plus-read-aloud with a native voice conversation for the same simple task.
Ask voice mode to tell a short story in two different styles and note where it succeeds or refuses.

lessons.title: NotebookLM podcasts
lessons.summary: NotebookLM lets you add source material, ask grounded questions, and generate a podcast-style discussion about those sources. Karpathy presents it as a way to explore niche material during passive listening.
objectives: Add documents or web sources to a notebook
Ask questions grounded in provided material
Generate and customize a deep-dive podcast
Use generated audio as an introduction rather than a definitive reference

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: NotebookLM places uploaded or linked sources into a notebook for chat and audio generation. Its deep-dive podcast feature creates a spoken discussion based on the notebook's material.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: A dense paper or niche subject can become something to listen to on a walk or drive, especially when no human-made podcast covers it. The same notebook also supports direct questions about its sources.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Create a notebook, add PDFs, web pages, or text, and ask questions about them. Use the podcast generation control to produce an audio overview; add special instructions to focus on an angle, regenerate, or use interactive mode to ask a question while listening.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Generation can take several minutes.
  • A generated overview is a convenient introduction, not expert verification.
  • Its usefulness is strongest for material you provide and niche topics that lack existing coverage.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Add one paper you want to understand, ask a source-grounded question, then generate a podcast with an instruction to explain the paper's central claim and evidence.

quotes.text: once you put this here, this enters the context window of the model
It's kind of like an AI podcast about any arbitrary niche topic you'd like.

images.caption: Sources are added to the notebook for grounding.
Podcast settings include instructions and interactive listening.
A generated series demonstrates the tool's audio format.

pitfalls: Expecting immediate generation
Treating a generated podcast as a substitute for checking source claims
Using it where a strong human-made podcast already serves the need
takeaways: Add sources before asking for source-grounded answers.
A podcast can make niche material easier to explore.
Steer the audio with special instructions.
Use the generated episode as a first exposure.
practice: Upload a short article or paper, ask two questions about it, and generate an audio overview with a specific angle.

lessons.title: Image input
lessons.summary: Vision-capable models turn image information into tokens they can process alongside text. For information-rich images, first ask for a transcription and verify it before asking for analysis.
objectives: Describe how images can enter a model as token sequences
Use a two-step transcribe-then-analyze workflow
Break long documents into manageable image sections
Treat high-stakes interpretations as a starting point for expert discussion

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: An image encoder represents visual content as tokens, such as patches, that the transformer can process alongside text. The model can therefore read screenshots, labels, equations, and other visual material.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: You can bring visual information directly into a conversation instead of retyping it. The key reliability step is checking what the model extracted before trusting its reasoning about the content.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Upload or paste the relevant image. First ask the model to transcribe the values or equation into text or a table. Check that transcription, then ask your substantive question about the verified text. For long documents, work one section at a time.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Visual transcription can misread small or unclear values.
  • Skipping verification makes errors harder to catch in a later analysis.
  • Medical explanations are a first draft and should prompt questions for a clinician, not replace one.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Use a screenshot of a chart or label. Request a text transcription, compare it against the original, and only then ask for a summary or comparison.

quotes.text: the reason I like to first transcribe the relevant information into text is because I want to make sure that the model is seeing the values correctly
I like to do it in two steps whenever possible.

images.caption: A visual label is used as a source for questions.
Transcribe the image before interpreting its values.
An equation can be converted into editable text.

pitfalls: Assuming the model read every number correctly
Analyzing an image without first checking its transcription
Using medical output instead of consulting a clinician
takeaways: Image inputs are represented as tokens the model can process.
Transcribe first, then ask questions.
Verify values against the original image.
Process multi-page material in sections.
Use medical interpretations to prepare questions for a doctor.
practice: Upload a chart or nutrition label; ask for a table, verify every entry, then ask one comparison question.
Convert a photographed equation to editable text and check symbols before using it.

lessons.title: Image output
lessons.summary: Image generation translates a text request into a visual result, often through a prompt or caption passed to a separate image model. Expect different tools to have different styles and strengths.
objectives: Describe the prompt-to-image workflow
Use a clear visual brief to request an image
Compare generated results across tools
Recognize that a text model may coordinate a separate image generator

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Image generation creates a picture from a text description. In the workflow Karpathy describes, the chat model can turn the request into a caption or prompt that is then sent to an image-generation model.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: You can ask for a visual concept without drawing it yourself. Different systems produce noticeably different styles and levels of quality, so the choice of tool can affect the result.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Describe the subject and the visual treatment you want, generate an image, and refine the prompt based on what is missing. If comparing tools, use the same prompt so their styles are easier to judge.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• The image may be produced by a separate model coordinated by the chat interface.
  • Different image tools have distinct styles and quality.
  • A first result may not match the prompt; iteration is part of the workflow.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Ask two image tools for the same simple scene, then refine one prompt by specifying the composition or style you want to change.

quotes.text: this will actually under the hood, create a caption for that image. And that caption is sent to a separate model that is an image generator model.
They all have a slightly different style, different quality, etc.

images.caption: The segment introduces text-prompted image generation.
A generated image illustrates the output workflow.
Different generators can have different visual styles.

pitfalls: Assuming the chat model itself directly renders pixels
Expecting all image tools to produce the same look
Treating the first generation as the final answer
takeaways: A text prompt can drive a separate image generator.
Describe both subject and desired visual treatment.
Compare tools with a consistent prompt.
Refine prompts when a result misses the brief.
practice: Generate the same scene in two tools and note differences in style and detail.
Revise the prompt once to change composition while keeping the subject fixed.

lessons.title: Video input
lessons.summary: Live camera input in advanced voice mode lets a person show a model objects or surroundings while speaking. The model may interpret video through sampled image frames rather than continuous human-like vision.
objectives: Use a live camera feed as conversational visual input
Ask spoken questions while showing an object
Understand that video may be processed as sampled frames
Keep camera-based interpretations appropriately cautious

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Video input in the demonstration is a live camera shared during a voice conversation. The user points the camera at things and asks the model about what it sees.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Camera input joins speech and vision in one interaction: instead of describing every object, you can show it and talk through the question.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Start a supported voice session, enable the camera, point it at the relevant object or scene, and ask a specific question. Keep the item visible and provide verbal context when needed.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• A smooth live experience does not mean the model sees every instant continuously.
  • The implementation may sample image sections or frames.
  • Changing camera conditions or a fleeting view can make visual interpretation uncertain.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Show the camera a familiar object and ask for a description, then ask one follow-up while changing the angle. Notice which details depend on a clear, steady view.

quotes.text: You basically have the camera running. You can point to that stuff and you can just talk to the model.
I think they actually still just take image sections. Maybe they take one image per second or something like that.

images.caption: The camera control starts a live visual interaction.
The user can point the camera while talking to the model.
The underlying system may sample frames from the video.

pitfalls: Assuming the model sees every video frame
Expecting it to infer details that are off-camera
Taking an uncertain visual guess as fact
takeaways: Live video enables show-and-ask voice interactions.
Keep the subject visible and ask a focused question.
Video may be represented by sampled images.
Give verbal context and verify uncertain observations.
practice: Use live camera input to ask about an object from two angles, then check whether the answer changes with visibility.

lessons.title: Video generation
lessons.summary: Video-generation systems can turn prompts into short clips, and the field is changing rapidly. Karpathy compares several systems using a shared tiger-in-a-jungle prompt to show their different results.
objectives: Recognize text-to-video as a rapidly evolving capability
Compare outputs using the same prompt
Notice differences in style and quality
Check current tools rather than relying on dated rankings

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Video generation uses a prompt to create a moving clip. The segment surveys multiple systems, including Sora and Veo 2, with a common example prompt.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Generated video can provide visual material from a short description, and the tools are improving quickly. Since each model has its own style and quality, comparing results is more useful than assuming one universal output.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Pick a concise scene, describe its subject and action, generate a clip, then adjust the prompt or try another generator. Compare tools with the same prompt and review their current capabilities.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Tool quality and availability can change quickly.
  • A model's style may differ from what the prompt implies.
  • The segment's dated comparison is not a permanent ranking.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Generate the same simple scene with two available systems and compare motion, consistency, and visual style.

quotes.text: a lot of tools now that can generate videos and they are incredible, and they're very rapidly evolving
They all have a slightly different style, different quality, etc.

images.caption: A shared prompt is used to compare generated clips.
The systems produce clips with distinct styles.

pitfalls: Treating a fast-changing model comparison as timeless
Comparing tools with different prompts
Assuming one prompt produces consistent results across generators
takeaways: Text-to-video is developing quickly.
Use a shared prompt to compare systems.
Judge motion, consistency, and style separately.
Recheck current capabilities before choosing a tool.
practice: Prompt two video generators with the same short scene and compare their outputs on motion and style.

lessons.title: ChatGPT memory
lessons.summary: Memory stores selected facts or preferences about a user so they can inform future chats. It is separate from the temporary context of an individual conversation and can be reviewed or edited.
objectives: Distinguish chat context from persistent memory
Ask the system to remember a durable preference
Review, edit, or delete saved memory
Consider privacy when choosing what to retain

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Memory is a list of text summaries about you that can persist across conversations. The talk describes it as a knowledge bank prepended to future chats, separate from the context in the current chat.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Persistent preferences can make repeated tasks, such as recommendations, more relevant without restating the same background each time.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: When a fact is useful across conversations, explicitly ask the assistant to remember it, or allow the feature to capture it where supported. Use the memory manager to inspect, edit, add, or delete entries.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Memory does not preserve every conversation automatically.
  • Do not confuse a chat's temporary context with information saved across chats.
  • Stored memories are personal data; choose carefully what you want retained.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Save one low-risk preference, start a new conversation, and check whether it is applied. Then open memory management and remove it.

quotes.text: a memory bank is basically a separate piece of Chachi PT that is kind of like a database of knowledge about you
this database of knowledge is always prepended to all the conversations so that the model has access to it

pitfalls: Assuming every detail will be remembered
Expecting temporary chat context to persist
Saving personal information without considering its sensitivity
takeaways: Memory is a persistent text store about the user.
It is distinct from the current conversation context.
Explicitly request important durable memories.
Review and edit saved entries periodically.
practice: Ask the assistant to remember a harmless preference, test it in a new chat, then delete it from the memory manager.

lessons.title: Custom instructions
lessons.summary: Custom instructions provide standing guidance about how an assistant should respond and what background about you matters. Because they apply across chats, reserve them for durable preferences.
objectives: Explain how custom instructions differ from per-chat prompts
Set global style and educational preferences
Add relevant background and language defaults
Keep global instructions concise and durable

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Custom instructions are persistent settings that shape an assistant's style and the user context it should consider across conversations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: A standing preference avoids repeating the same direction in every chat. Karpathy's examples include conversational tone, educational explanations, and a consistent formality level for Korean.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html: Open the app's customization settings and add a few direct rules about response style and durable background. For example, specify whether you prefer plain language or a particular language register.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• Instructions affect many conversations, so avoid directions that only apply to one task.
  • Without a preferred register, language tone can vary.
  • Equivalent settings may be named differently in other apps.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Write one style preference and one useful background detail. Test them in a new conversation, then revise anything too broad or restrictive.

quotes.text: just don't be like an HR business partner. Just talk to me normally.
anything you want to modify about chat GPT globally between conversations, you would kind of put it here into your custom instructions.

pitfalls: Putting one-off task directions in global settings
Leaving important language tone preferences implicit
Assuming every app uses the same settings name
takeaways: Custom instructions apply across conversations.
Use them for stable style and personal context.
Specify tone or language register when it matters.
Look for equivalent settings in other LLM apps.
practice: Add a concise global preference, try it in a new chat, and edit it if the response style is too broad.

lessons.title: Custom GPTs
lessons.summary: A custom GPT packages a reusable prompt for a recurring task. Clear task instructions plus concrete examples can reduce repeated setup and help the model follow a consistent output format.
objectives: Identify a repetitive prompt worth saving
Build instructions from background, task, and examples
Use few-shot examples to demonstrate desired outputs
Structure multi-step workflows explicitly

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: Custom GPTs are saved configurations built from prompting. They can include context, task instructions, and example inputs and outputs; the feature saves the effort of pasting the same prompt repeatedly.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: Examples make the desired behavior concrete. Karpathy demonstrates Korean vocabulary extraction into Anki-ready pairs and a translator that gives a full translation followed by a detailed breakdown.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html:
Start with a repeated task. In the GPT instructions, state relevant background, define the task and output format, and include several representative examples. For a multi-step image task, spell out the sequence, such as OCR, translation, then explanation.

Delimit longer examples clearly, using tags if helpful, so their boundaries are obvious.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• A custom GPT is a prompt configuration, not a fundamentally different model.
  • Vague instructions without examples can produce inconsistent output.
  • Do not assume a custom GPT configuration is portable to every app.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: Turn a prompt you reuse into a small custom GPT. Add two input-output examples and test it with a new input that was not in the examples.

quotes.text: This is all just done via prompting. Nothing special is happening here.
what this feature really is, is that it's just saving you prompting time.
it's so much better if you show them by example how to perform the task.

pitfalls: Expecting the GPT feature to add special model capabilities
Relying on a vague zero-shot task description
Leaving example boundaries unclear
Assuming the setup works identically outside its platform
takeaways: Save a prompt when you repeatedly perform the same task.
Combine background, a specific task, and output requirements.
Show desired behavior with concrete examples.
Break complex workflows into explicit steps.
Test examples against new inputs.
practice: Build a reusable prompt configuration for a repeated task, including two clear input-output examples.
Test it on a fresh case and adjust instructions where output diverges from the example.

lessons.title: The practical LLM checklist
lessons.summary: The talk closes with a changing ecosystem of apps and a practical map for choosing models and tools. Match the app and model to the task, use reasoning and tools deliberately, and keep experimenting as capabilities shift.
objectives: Choose an LLM app by its strengths and the task at hand
Check model size and tier before judging an answer
Escalate to reasoning models when ordinary models struggle
Select tools for current information, computation, and creation
Recognize modality and platform differences

sections.heading: What it is
sections.html: The LLM app ecosystem is competitive: ChatGPT is a strong default, while other apps can excel at particular jobs. The talk's mental models connect model size, reasoning, tools, multimodal input and output, and quality-of-life features.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.html: The model and app behind a chat affect what it knows and how it performs. A small model may be less knowledgeable or more prone to mistakes; search, Python, and creative tools can extend what the model can do.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.html:
1. Identify the task and choose an app suited to it.
  2. Check which model and tier you are using.
  3. Try a standard model first; switch to a reasoning model if a hard math, code, or logic task remains unsolved.
  4. Use search for fresh facts, Python for calculations and plots, and creation tools for prototypes or media.
  5. Check whether needed voice, image, or video features are available on your current platform.

sections.heading: Pitfalls & misconceptions
sections.html:
• No single app is best at every task.
  • Fresh information may not be in a model's training data; use search.
  • Reasoning mode is not necessary for every request.
  • Features can differ between web and mobile, and multimodal systems may handle media natively or through separate tools.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.html: For your next task, write down the job, the model and tier, any tool needed, and what you will verify. If the first approach fails, change one part of the setup and try again.

quotes.text: you're talking basically to a zip file.
try without reasoning first. And if your model is not solving that kind of a problem, try to switch to a reasoning model
all of this is a little bit of a zoo.

pitfalls: Assuming one app is best for every use
Ignoring the selected model and plan tier
Using reasoning mode by default for easy requests
Expecting training data to include fresh facts
Assuming features are identical across web and mobile
takeaways: Choose an app for its task-specific strengths; keep a capable default for general use.
Know your model and tier because capability varies.
Try without reasoning first, then escalate when the task needs it.
Use search for current facts and Python for calculations or plots.
Check whether multimodal features are native or tool-mediated, and whether the platform supports them.
Experiment over time as the app ecosystem changes.
practice: Use the checklist on one real task: choose an app and model, decide whether search or another tool is needed, and verify one key claim.
Try a task first without reasoning; if it fails, switch to a reasoning model and compare the results.

glossary.definition: A neural network trained to emit tokens; as Karpathy puts it, it is inert and has no tools until the application gives it some.
The token window holding the current conversation and material supplied or fetched for the model to use as working memory.
The current context window: conversation tokens and loaded information directly available to the model during the exchange.
The one-dimensional sequence of tokens that user and model build turn by turn in a chat.
Training on internet text through next-token prediction, compressing learned patterns into model parameters.
Training with human-built conversations that shapes the model into an assistant persona.
The limit on how current the model's stored training knowledge can be; later information must be supplied or retrieved.
A fabricated or incorrect output that can sound plausible, including claims accompanied by citations.
The model emits special tokens requesting an action, the application runs a tool, and the result returns as text in context.
An application capability that searches the web, loads fetched pages into context, and lets the model continue its answer.
A long-running combination of internet search and thinking that produces a cited, report-length synthesis.
A model or mode that deliberates before answering; the talk describes normal and extended options and associates extra thinking with harder tasks.
The original or authoritative source used to check a claim, such as the product box Karpathy compared with an answer.
A code execution tool that runs a program written by the model and returns its output to the conversation.
A ChatGPT feature that lets the model gather data, run analysis code, plot results, and fit or extrapolate trends.
A Claude feature in which the model writes code, such as a React app, that the interface runs in the browser.
A diagram library whose text definitions Claude can generate and render as conceptual graphs.
Cursor's autonomous coding agent that can execute commands and edit multiple files in a project.
Karpathy's phrase for giving control to Composer, describing the desired outcome, and hoping the agent's changes work.
Karpathy's informal name for asking several language models the same question and comparing their answers.
